claims.text: Superconducting critical temperature in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the degree of chemical disorder.
Chemical disorder modulates electron-phonon coupling through local lattice distortions.
Increased disorder disrupts the uniformity of atomic bonding.
Disruption of uniform atomic bonding reduces the effective superconducting pairing interaction.
The initial alloy is homogeneous and contains randomly distributed constituent elements.
Composition or processing can be varied to create higher- and lower-disorder samples while preserving average electron count and crystal structure.
Changes in configurational disorder induce changes in local atomic ordering and associated lattice distortions.
Chemical disorder affects the phonon spectrum.
Higher disorder introduces local lattice distortions that reduce the coherence of the electron-phonon interaction needed for Cooper pairing.
Reduced coherence of the electron-phonon interaction suppresses superconducting critical temperature.
Samples with enhanced chemical disorder will have a lower critical temperature than the baseline alloy.
Reducing chemical disorder will correlate with an increase in critical temperature when other pairing mechanisms do not dominate.
The proposed mechanism should mainly apply to alloys whose superconductivity is driven by electron-phonon interactions.
Magnetic fluctuations or extrinsic factors may obscure or eliminate the effect of disorder on critical temperature.
Residual stresses and microstructural defects may also influence superconductivity.
X-ray diffraction, atom-probe tomography, diffraction-based ordering parameters, or pair-distribution-function analysis can be used to quantify disorder or local ordering.
A lack of a consistent relationship between quantified disorder and critical temperature would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention proposes altering alloy composition, whereas the conditions require overall stoichiometry to remain constant and only configurational disorder to vary.

The conditions require identical processing histories, but the experiment proposes different thermal treatments to promote ordering; those treatments necessarily create different processing histories.

Adding an ordering-promoting element or changing elemental ratios is presented as a way to vary only disorder, but it also changes chemical composition and may change average electron count or other electronic variables.
